title: Blood libels
hook: false accusations beginning in Norwich led to killings; some popes condemned them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiddush Hashem: a jewel carried back to its owner. Your line was sanctify the name by living. Today, the end of the week, and what a lie can do.

Easter week in Norwich, England. A boy named William is found dead in a wood outside the town. Nobody knows who killed him. Years later a monk named Thomas of Monmouth writes a book claiming the Jews of Norwich did it, in mockery of the crucifixion. There is no evidence. His sources are rumor, dreams and a convert's word. But the book spreads, the boy becomes a local saint, and the story finds a shape that will be told again and again in other towns.
screen: `A BOY FOUND IN A WOOD.` → `A MONK'S BOOK.` → `A STORY THAT TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: A libel is a false and damaging accusation. The blood libel is the false claim that Jews murder Christian children, and in later tellings that they use the blood in their rituals, often around Passover. Every part of it is false, and it runs straight against Jewish law, which forbids eating blood at all. The Torah repeats the ban, and the rules of kosher meat are built around removing blood. Yet the story kept returning. When a child went missing or a body was found, someone remembered the tale, and Jews were arrested, tortured into confessions, or killed by crowds. Not everyone believed it. Some popes wrote against it. Pope Innocent the Fourth, answering complaints from Jewish communities in Germany, wrote that Jews were being falsely accused of eating the hearts of murdered children, when their own law forbids such things. Some rulers issued similar protections. But a lie that people want to believe outruns a letter. The Torah has a short rule about this, in Leviticus: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." The same verse goes on to forbid standing idly by while a neighbor's blood is shed. Some readers hear the two halves together: careless words can end in harm. This week ran from riots in Spain, through Rabbeinu Gershom's rulings, Rashi and his daughters, the Rhineland and Kiddush Hashem, to this. The blood libel sits underneath much of it: a story told without evidence can cost lives.
screen: `A FALSE ACCUSATION.` · `AGAINST JEWISH LAW ITSELF.` · `SOME POPES WROTE AGAINST IT.` · then, large: `NO TALEBEARING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've heard lately about a person or a group that you can't actually check: a forwarded message, a headline, a bit of gossip. Notice the pull to repeat it, then picture letting it stop with you, not sent and not added to.
Blood libels. False stories that Jews killed children for ritual purposes, told from Norwich onward, condemned by some popes, and believed by crowds anyway. Today's word.
Your line: lies kill. And a rumor that reaches you can stop with you. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats gossip and talebearing (lashon hara and rechilut) as serious wrongs, and some Jews study these laws to guard what they say about others.

chat.says: Where did the blood libel story even come from? Was any of it true?
options: None of it; it grew from rumor, and Jewish law forbids eating blood at all.
Partly; it began with a real court case that found Jews guilty in Norwich.
Nobody knows; the monk's book about it was lost long ago.
